1) **Services**

### **The sum or selection of these services makeup a complete greenhouse solution** {#the-sum-or-selection-of-these-services-makeup-a-complete-greenhouse-solution}

### **1.1) Site and crop viability assessment** {#1.1)-site-and-crop-viability-assessment}

We assess light levels across your site in summer and winter to understand what you can grow, where, and when. The assessment also helps determine whether supplementary lighting or climate control would be useful for your chosen crops.

### **1.2) Climate management design** {#1.2)-climate-management-design}

Each greenhouse is designed around its location and intended crops. Temperature and humidity sensors can control extraction fans, while heat activated vents provide passive ventilation when conditions allow. Vent size, placement and outside weather still determine how much cooling passive ventilation can provide.

### **1.3) Root zone and irrigation planning** {#1.3)-root-zone-and-irrigation-planning}

Choose from soil beds, raised beds and hydroponic systems, including deep water culture and nutrient film technique. Where nearby trees or hedges compete for water and nutrients, raised or isolated beds can protect the growing area. Moisture sensors can help schedule irrigation so roots receive water while retaining the air they need to grow.

### **1.4) Integrated pest management strategies** {#1.4)-integrated-pest-management-strategies}

We develop a plant protection plan around your crops and the pests present on site. Regular monitoring, good growing practices and suitable biological controls form the foundation. Depending on your approach, the plan may also include compatible treatments when needed.

### **1.5) Supplementary lighting** {#1.5)-supplementary-lighting}

In shaded locations or seasons with limited daylight, supplementary LEDs can extend the growing period or provide the light a crop needs to perform well. We size lighting around the crop’s daily light requirement and the natural light available. Solar and battery systems can supply some or all of the electricity, depending on their capacity and the lighting demand.

### **1.6) Monitoring and control** {#1.6)-monitoring-and-control}

A locally hosted, web connected control system lets you check greenhouse conditions remotely, operate compatible irrigation and ventilation equipment, and receive alerts when readings move outside your chosen ranges.

### **1.7) Training and guidance** {#1.7)-training-and-guidance}

We offer onsite training for owners and staff, from hands-on growing basics to more detailed system management. This can cover germination, transplanting, hydroponic reservoirs, crop monitoring and routine maintenance, supported by a digital or printed guide.

2) ## **Essential plant growth concepts** {#essential-plant-growth-concepts}

### **2.1) Light** {#2.1)-light}

Light supplies the energy for photosynthesis. How well a plant uses that light also depends on its temperature, water supply, nutrients and growing conditions.

### **2.2) Temperature** {#2.2)-temperature}

Every crop has a temperature range in which it grows well. A greenhouse helps manage conditions throughout the day and across the seasons, increasing the time crops spend within a suitable range.

### **2.3) Vapour pressure deficit** {#2.3)-vapour-pressure-deficit}

Vapour pressure deficit, or VPD, describes the difference between the moisture in the air and the amount it could hold when saturated. It helps explain how readily water moves from leaves into the air. Temperature and relative humidity can be used to estimate VPD, but the most suitable range depends on the crop and its stage of growth. Conditions that are too dry can increase water stress, while overly humid conditions can restrict transpiration and encourage some diseases.

### **2.4) Water and root zone** {#2.4)-water-and-root-zone}

Plants need both water and oxygen around their roots. Waterlogged conditions reduce the oxygen available to roots, while dry conditions limit growth and can cause water stress. Irrigation sensors help inform watering decisions, with settings adjusted to the specific crop, soil or substrate in real time rather than relying on a single schedule.

### **2.5) Climate steering and zoning** {#2.5)-climate-steering-and-zoning}

Different crops and growth stages can favour different conditions. Planting leafy greens in a cooler, shadier area and sun loving crops in a brighter area makes use of the variation already present in a greenhouse. Where crops need more distinct conditions, partitions and separately controlled zones may help. A climate guide can set out suitable temperature, humidity and ventilation targets for your equipment and chosen crops.

3) ## **Materials and growing systems** {#materials-and-growing-systems}

### **3.1) Material choice** {#3.1)-material-choice}

Greenhouses can range from bespoke timber and glass structures to prefabricated aluminium and polycarbonate kits. Appearance and budget matter, but site conditions, light transmission, ventilation and how the greenhouse is managed also shape growing performance.

### **3.2) Timber or steel and glass** {#3.2)-timber-or-steel-and-glass}

A custom timber or steel frame with suitable greenhouse glazing can offer a distinctive appearance and a long service life. Costs depend on the structure, glazing specification and fabrication required.

### **3.3) Timber and polycarbonate** {#3.3)-timber-and-polycarbonate}

Timber allows a frame to be tailored to existing structures and the character of the property. Twin wall polycarbonate can offer insulation and diffuse incoming light, though light transmission and service life vary by product.

### **3.4) Aluminium and polycarbonate kits** {#3.4)-aluminium-and-polycarbonate-kits}

Prefabricated kits can be a practical option where their dimensions suit the site. Foundations, raised beds and any supporting structure need to be considered as part of the full installation cost.

### **3.5) Substrate and container options** {#3.5)-substrate-and-container-options}

* Growing in the existing soil  
* Framed beds with a selected growing mix  
* Fully raised beds  
* Hydroponics, including deep water culture, nutrient film technique or stonewool.

### **3.6) Supplementary lighting** {#3.6)-supplementary-lighting}

Where a site receives limited light, crops can be selected to suit the conditions or supported with artificial lighting. LEDs can extend the day or add light during darker periods. Existing solar and battery infrastructure may help, but the choice depends on when the lights run and how much electricity the system can supply.

### **3.7) Additional facilities** {#3.7)-additional-facilities}

**Germination station:** A dedicated space with suitable temperature, light and humidity for starting seedlings.

**Postharvest area:** Space for washing, preparing and drying harvested produce, designed around the crops and intended use.

7) Climate Steering

Greenhouse **climate steering** optimizes not only plant growth, but also boosts the production of secondary metabolites in vegetable and herb crops by applying controlled, mild abiotic stress (known as intentional elicitation). In a controlled environment agriculture (CEA) system, growers strategically adjust climate parameters to trigger the plant's natural defense mechanisms. This shifts metabolic resources away from vegetative growth (primary metabolism) and toward the synthesis of protective phytochemicals (secondary metabolism) without causing lasting damage or critical yield loss. \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12202592/), [2](https://ipp.farm/secondary-metabolites-production-in-controlled-environment-agriculture/), [3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0885576525003443), [4](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/413737006_Environmental_Control_and_Controlled_Elicitation_Strategies_to_Modulate_Phytochemical_Quality_of_Medicinal_and_Aromatic_Plants_in_Controlled_Environment_Agriculture)\]

How Climate Steering Drives Synthesis

Plants synthesize secondary metabolites to acclimate to environmental shifts, scavenge reactive oxygen species (ROS), and stabilize cellular structures. Greenhouses manipulate these responses through four main environmental levers: \[[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44372-026-00770-2), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9920071/), [3](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/12/3/447)\]

* **Light Quality & Intensity (Photobiology):** Supplementing with **UV-B radiation** acts as an energetic stressor, rapidly upregulating the *phenylpropanoid pathway* to produce protective antioxidants. Altering the **Red to Far-Red (R:FR)** or increasing **blue light** ratios triggers photoreceptor signaling, which directly shifts terpene and phenolic concentrations. \[[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4395/16/17/1652), [2](https://ipp.farm/secondary-metabolites-production-in-controlled-environment-agriculture/), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44372-026-00770-2), [4](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/367260423_Environmental_Factors_Regulate_Plant_Secondary_Metabolites)\]  
* **Temperature Manipulation:** Introducing moderate temperature drops (cold stress) or restricted heat spikes activates transcription factors (like *MYB* or *WRKY*). This accelerates the transcription of key biosynthetic enzymes, altering the plant's chemical composition. \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11838150/), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9920071/), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12202592/), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12029941/)\]  
* **Controlled Water Deficit (VPD & Irrigation):** Intentionally lowering greenhouse relative humidity or stretching irrigation intervals spikes the **Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD)**. This mild drought stress restricts osmotic potential, prompting the plant to mass-produce protective compounds to prevent water loss and oxidative damage. \[[1](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/399300978_Influence_of_environmental_stress_on_secondary_metabolite_production_in_plants), [2](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/14/21/3390), [3](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/367260423_Environmental_Factors_Regulate_Plant_Secondary_Metabolites), [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44372-026-00770-2)\]  
* **Carbon Dioxide Enrichment:** Elevating greenhouse $C{O}_{2}$ increases photosynthetic carbon assimilation. This generates an "energy overflow" or high carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio, leaving excess carbon available to be funneled directly into carbon-rich non-nitrogenous metabolites. \[[1](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2019.01463/full), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11659182/), [3](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/367260423_Environmental_Factors_Regulate_Plant_Secondary_Metabolites), [4](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/gcb.16484)\]

8.2) Botanical Library

Botanical Library \- **Original Text**

Climate stability and resilience, a biosphere to sustain a unique collection of endemic, endangered or exotic plants. A botanical library can include more than just a cultivation environment, but also one designed around conservation, seed saving and propagation.

Crop types include; Dias’s, Sundews, Bromeliads, Orchids ferns

- Drosera capensis  
- Drosera regia  
- [Drosera admirabilis](https://www.fierceflora.com/finding-every-described-sundew-in-the-western-cape-south-africa/) & [Drosera aliciae](https://pza.sanbi.org/drosera-aliciae)  
- [**Adiantum capillus-veneris**](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fm%2F02kw75&q=Adiantum+capillus-veneris) **(Cape Maidenhair Fern):** The quintessential waterfall fern. It clings directly to wet, vertical rock faces in deep gorges, constantly bathed in fine waterfall spray. \[[1](https://wildflowernursery.co.za/indigenous-plant-database/wpbdp_category/fern/)\]  
- [**Blechnum capense**](https://www.google.com/search?q=Blechnum+capense) **(Cape Blechnum / Deer Fern):** A robust fern with striking, arching fronds that forms dense colonies along shaded stream banks and mountain seeps. \[[1](https://www.gardenandhome.co.za/gardening/how-tos/6-of-the-best-ferns-2/)\]  
- [**Rumohra adiantiformis**](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fm%2F066182l&q=Rumohra+adiantiformis) **(Seven-weeks Fern / Leatherleaf Fern):** Thrives in moist, dark forest margins and wet rocky areas from the Cape Peninsula upwards. \[[1](https://pza.sanbi.org/dryopteridaceae), [2](https://wildflowernursery.co.za/indigenous-plant-database/wpbdp_category/fern/)\]  
- [**Alsophila capensis**](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fhkb%2FCg4KCGxhbmd1YWdlEgJlbgoOCgR0eXBlEgZBTklNQUwKIQoLZW50aXR5X25hbWUSEmFsc29waGlsYSBjYXBlbnNpcw%3D%3D&q=Alsophila+capensis) **(Cape Tree Fern):** For a dramatic look, this beautiful tree fern grows natively along cool forest rivers and mist-heavy mountain ravines. \[[1](https://www.thegardener.co.za/the-gardener/ferns/garden-ferns-2/), [2](https://www.gardenandhome.co.za/gardening/how-tos/6-of-the-best-ferns-2/)\]

A little ecosystem of your own, where plants and people can thrive together.

# 9\. ) Botanical Library Specs {#9.-)-botanical-library-specs}

# Cultivation Parameters by Crop Group {#cultivation-parameters-by-crop-group}

To replicate a South African waterfall climate at home or in a greenhouse, group your plants by their specific environmental targets. The most critical factor across all groups is **keeping the root systems cool**, even if the ambient air warms up. \[[1](https://www.getgrowli.app/plant-care/disa-uniflora), [2](https://www.burymeinthebog.com/grow/king-sundews?srsltid=AU7gw4UqzoHvI_icD52HqQqa6YUuUrs4z0LqSn03Mssf64sPjdxwwgvB)\]

**Group 1: The Waterfall Orchids ([*Disa uniflora*](https://www.google.com/search?q=Disa+uniflora))**

While they can tolerate a surprisingly high amount of light in nature due to the cold water rushing over their roots, they require careful temperature control in cultivation to prevent root rot. \[[1](https://oscov.asn.au/articles/growing-disa-uniflora-and-its-hybrids-by-brian-milligan/), [2](https://www.getgrowli.app/plant-care/disa-uniflora), [3](https://travaldo.blogspot.com/2018/04/disa-uniflora-care-and-culture.html)\]

* **DLI / Sun Hours:** **6–12 mol/m²/day**. Under natural conditions, this translates to bright, indirect light or morning sun (**3–4 sun hours**). In a controlled setup, target 20,000–30,000 lux.  
* **Humidity:** **65% – 85%**. They demand high atmospheric moisture but absolute **constant air movement**. Stagnant, humid air will quickly cause crown rot.  
* **Temperature:** Day: **18°C – 25°C** | Night: **10°C – 15°C**. *Critical Rule:* Root temperatures must strictly stay below 21°C; use chilled, pure water (Rain/RO) to flush pots on warm days. \[[1](https://seedstudiosf.com/blogs/blogs/all-about-disa-seed-studio), [2](https://travaldo.blogspot.com/2018/04/disa-uniflora-care-and-culture.html), [3](https://oscov.asn.au/articles/growing-disa-uniflora-and-its-hybrids-by-brian-milligan/), [4](https://www.getgrowli.app/plant-care/disa-uniflora)\]

# 10.)  Flavour & Nutrition: Commercial vs Boutique Crop Selection  {#10.)-flavour-&-nutrition:-commercial-vs-boutique-crop-selection}

**H**omegrown vegetables and herbs are typically healthier and higher in vitamins, antioxidants and phytonutrients than store-bought produce. Most nutrients start degrading the moment produce is harvested, and store-bought vegetables are often picked before peak ripeness to survive shipping and long storage windows. 

Most commercial varieties are selected to offer high aesthetic appeal, easy handling and stable shelf life, unfortunately crops selected for these characteristics, coupled with premature harvesting almost always comes at the cost of flavour, aroma and nutrition. 

11.) Climate resilience, Food security   
While producing food at home may not move the needle in the global battle against food-insecurity, we can all start at home when it comes to reducing the footprint or our culinary consumption. 

# 12.) Eat What you grow \- grow what you eat  {#12.)-eat-what-you-grow---grow-what-you-eat}

* **Self-reliance:** Growing your own produce can give you more control over your food supply and nutrition, while reducing your dependence on grocery stores.  
* **Freshness and Flavor:** Homegrown produce can be picked at peak ripeness rather than harvested early for long-distance transport, which makes it taste better and hold more nutrients.  
* **Health and Safety:** You decide what goes into the soil and onto your plants, meaning you can avoid unwanted synthetic pesticides, herbicides or post-harvest whose long term health risks have been, and are becoming clearer. Taking control over your own food supply is one of the first steps you can take to help promote your health and that of your family. 

# 13.) ~~Social Upliftment~~  {#13.)-social-upliftment}

~~As our business grows, we are committed to developing healthy and secure food production systems for isolated communities who often lack access to fresh nutrition produce or those stuck in the urban sprawl without the means to support a healthy diet for themselves and their loved ones.~~

~~Together we can help increase food security and the quality of living, as aided through healthy nutrition to those most in need.~~ 

As our business grows, we are committed to developing healthy and secure food production systems for those in need.

Isolated communities who often lack access to fresh nutrition produce are often not limited by space by by cultivation resources and in some cases expertise. While those stuck in the urban sprawl are almost always without the space, time and means to afford themselves and their loved ones a healthy diet so needed, not just to survive, but to thrive and grow.

While these challenges require different approaches, the intersection of food systems, technology with applied social and environmental science are at the core of the solutions that can help drive positive change for both people and planet.

If you have a specific project idea, or community in mind, please reach out\! 

Together we can help increase food security and the quality of living, as aided through healthy nutrition to those most in need.
